                    ### Question
                    A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of progressively worsening shortness of breath with exertion and intermittent palpitations over the last 2 months. She has had neither chest pain nor a cough. Her pulse is 124/min and irregular. Physical examination shows a grade 4/6 high-pitched holosystolic murmur that is best heard at the apex and radiates to the back. The murmur increases in intensity when she clenches her hands into fists. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Pulmonary artery thrombus on computed tomography scan
opb. Diffuse ST elevations on electrocardiogram
opc. Obstruction of the right marginal artery on coronary angiogram
opd. Reversible area of myocardial ischemia on nuclear stress test
ope. Dilation of left atrium on echocardiogram

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with progressively worsening shortness of breath and palpitations, with an irregular pulse suggestive of atrial fibrillation. The high-pitched holosystolic murmur at the apex indicates mitral regurgitation, which can lead to volume overload and subsequently cause left atrial dilation. This is supported by the consensus that mitral regurgitation is associated with left atrial enlargement due to increased left atrial pressure. Therefore, the most likely finding on further evaluation, particularly echocardiography, would be dilation of the left atrium. Other options, such as pulmonary artery thrombus, ST elevations, coronary obstruction, or reversible ischemia, are less likely given the clinical presentation and findings. Thus, the best-supported conclusion is that the echocardiogram will show dilation of the left atrium.
